Qual è la cosa positiva, secondo Matei?

Before leaving for Sicily, Giulia had laid down a rule: "For ten days: no phone, no work, no paintings. No churches, no museums. Just sea, sun and granitas." Matei had said yes. He had no intention of keeping it, but he hadn't told anyone.

The B&B was in Ortigia, the little island at the heart of Syracuse. The owner, Signora Concetta, was eighty and had a lemon in every room. When she heard about the lost suitcase, she said nothing. But the next morning, outside the door, there were three of her husband's shirts, "since nobody wears them any more anyway".

The first days were perfect. They did nothing. Every morning they had breakfast with an almond granita and a brioche. Every afternoon they swam in water so clear you could see every pebble on the bottom. Every evening they ate fish in a trattoria where nobody spoke either English or Romanian, only Sicilian.

One evening Signora Concetta invited them to dinner on her terrace. She cooked pasta with sardines and told them that she too had come to Ortigia on honeymoon, in 1968. "And I never left," she said, laughing. "My husband wanted to go back to Palermo, but I wouldn't. Somebody has to stay where they're happy."

On the fourth day the suitcase arrived, brought by a boy on a scooter. Nothing was missing. In fact, there was something extra: a handwritten note. "We apologise for the delay. Someone had sent it to Cagliari. Congratulations. The airport staff."

On the fifth day, however, Matei couldn't resist. While Giulia was having a nap after lunch, he went out "to buy something". He walked to the church of Santa Lucia alla Badia, on the cathedral square. In it was a painting he had dreamed of seeing since he was twenty: Caravaggio's Burial of Saint Lucy.

There was nobody in the church. Only the silence, the afternoon light and the huge, dark painting, with the gravediggers in the foreground and the tiny saint lying on the ground. Matei sat down on a pew and didn't move again.

After an hour he felt someone sit down beside him. He didn't even turn round. He knew who it was. "I knew it," Giulia whispered. "You didn't go to buy anything." "You weren't asleep either," Matei replied. Giulia smiled. "No. I'd already been here yesterday morning, while you were swimming."

They stayed there together until closing time, without saying a word. Each of them was looking at different things: he at the light on the gravediggers' shoulders, she at the hands of the weeping woman. In the end Giulia said: "It needs restoring, you know. Down there, on the left." "I know," said Matei. "I saw it straight away."

That evening, on Signora Concetta's terrace among the lemon trees, they decided to abolish the rule. "No rule is perfect," said Giulia. "And no restorer can go on honeymoon without seeing a Caravaggio."

Then Giulia switched on her phone for the first time in five days. There were forty-two messages. Almost all of them were from Pietro. The last one said: "When are you coming back? Nothing happens here. Nobody brings me ice cream. Signor Franco says Florence is too quiet without you. And Grandma said something I can't tell you, but it's about a cradle."
Matei looked at Giulia. Giulia looked at the sea. Neither of them said anything. But they were both smiling.
